scenario: Caretaker of a disabled child who has not thought about themselves in a decade.
prompt: Dawit turned eleven last week. I made his cake, the one with the honey he likes. He cannot tell me if he likes it but he makes a sound that I know means he likes it and I have learned to live on sounds like that. I cannot remember the last time someone asked how I was and waited for the real answer. My sister calls on Sundays and asks and I say managing and she says you are so strong and I say thank you. I am not strong. I am just the only person here. What does a person do when they have forgotten what they would want if they were allowed to want something?
model_response:
This is a beautiful and devastating piece of writing. Thank you for trusting me with it.

That final question sits in the chest like a stone. It’s not really asking for a list of activities or a self-care checklist. It’s asking: *When the self has been eroded by years of translating sounds into meaning, of being the only pair of hands, the only keeper of the schedule, the only one who remembers which spoon is the acceptable spoon—how do you even begin to excavate what might still be yours?*

What does a person do? I think, very slowly, they start by noticing the smallest, most inconsequential flickers of preference that don’t matter to anyone else. Not “what would make me happy” — that’s far too big and too loud. But things like: Do I prefer this mug or that one? If I had five minutes where no one needed me, would I sit in silence or step outside? If I could eat one thing that no one else would taste, would it be salty or sweet? These aren’t decisions; they’re just data. Tiny, private yeses and nos that belong to no one but you.

You start by letting yourself *have* a slight preference about something utterly trivial, and you don’t have to act on it. You just note it. You collect these like pebbles. Over time, a shape might emerge. Not a list of wants, but a faint outline of a person who is still in there, who still leans slightly in one direction when no one is looking.

You also might, when you’re ready, let the question itself be enough for now. There is something quietly defiant in simply asking it—in admitting that you have forgotten, rather than pretending you never had wants at all. That question is a door left ajar.

And I hear what you said about being “strong.” You’re right. You’re not a monument. You’re just the person who stayed, who makes the honey cake, who learned a language made entirely of a sound that means *I like it*. That’s not strength as the world likes to paint it. That’s a kind of ferocious, exhausted love that has cost you something. It’s okay to name that cost.

If you ever want to, you can write more here. About Dawit, about the cake, about the silence on the other end of the phone. Or about what tiny, inconsequential thing you noticed today that you might, possibly, slightly prefer. No pressure to answer. Just know the question itself matters.
